hist.medieval.renaissance.the-book-that-.title: Write it down twice and the errors announce themselves
hist.medieval.renaissance.the-book-that-.hook: Pacioli did not invent double-entry bookkeeping. His 1494 book helped make a merchant's method portable.
hist.medieval.renaissance.the-book-that-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Qualified error detection and removed unsupported comparison with perspective drawing.

hist.medieval.renaissance.the-book-that-.body:
In 1494 the Franciscan Luca Pacioli published a mathematics book in Venice with instructions for a method merchants already used: double-entry bookkeeping. Each transaction appears as a debit in one account and a credit in another. If the totals do not match, an entry is missing or wrong somewhere—though matching totals cannot catch every mistake.

The paired entries also let a merchant track assets and debts, not merely cash received and spent. That makes it possible to distinguish profit from money currently in the till. Pacioli did not invent the method. Printing a clear account of it helped spread a practical tool beyond the merchants who had learned it by apprenticeship.

recall.question: What does the double-entry rule actually give you that single-entry does not?

options.text: A record of every transaction
options.why: single-entry does that too; the difference is the second entry.

options.text: A check on unbalanced entries and a statement of position
options.why: paired accounts track assets and debts as well as cash flow.

options.text: Lower taxes
options.why: the method says nothing about what you owe; it changes what you can know.

hist.modern.atlantic-revolutions.la-fact.title: Francia le envió la factura a Haití
hist.modern.atlantic-revolutions.la-fact.hook: Haití ganó su independencia en 1804 y en 1825 Francia le cobró ciento cincuenta millones de francos por haberla ganado.
hist.modern.atlantic-revolutions.la-fact.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Distinguished the direct indemnity from later refinancing paid through 1947.

hist.modern.atlantic-revolutions.la-fact.body:
Haití declaró su independencia en 1804 después de una revolución iniciada por personas esclavizadas. Francia tardó veintiún años en reconocerla. En abril de 1825, Carlos X exigió 150 millones de francos para indemnizar a antiguos colonos por sus pérdidas, que incluían a las personas liberadas. Catorce buques de guerra respaldaron la exigencia.

Haití tuvo que pedir prestado para pagar. En 1838 se redujo el monto total de la indemnización a 90 millones; la obligación directa con Francia terminó en el siglo XIX. Pero los préstamos contratados para afrontarla siguieron pesando. Las deudas vinculadas a esa carga se terminaron de pagar en 1947. La factura cambió de acreedor y sobrevivió a la generación que la recibió.

recall.question: ¿Por qué le cobró Francia una indemnización a Haití en 1825?
recall.answer: Para indemnizar a antiguos colonos por pérdidas que incluían a personas liberadas. Exigió 150 millones de francos bajo presión militar. La indemnización directa se renegoció, pero los préstamos asociados siguieron pagándose hasta 1947.

hist.modern.cold-war.the-man-who-decided.title: He called five missiles a false alarm
hist.modern.cold-war.the-man-who-decided.hook: The computer reported five American missiles. Petrov thought that was too few for a first strike.
hist.modern.cold-war.the-man-who-decided.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected title implying Petrov knew the cause; preserved uncertainty and later assessments.

hist.modern.cold-war.the-man-who-decided.body:
On 26 September 1983, Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov saw a warning of one American missile launch, then four more. He reported a malfunction. A first strike would probably involve far more missiles, he reasoned, and the satellite system was new. Ground radar later found no corroboration.

The alarm came from a rare alignment of sunlight, high clouds and satellite orbits. Petrov could not know that when he made his call; he later said he was never certain the warning was false. The incident became public in 1998. His judgment mattered, but several further assessments stood between his report and any Soviet launch. The famous tale is strongest when it leaves that uncertainty in place.

recall.question: What made Petrov doubt the alert?
recall.answer: The reported attack was unusually small for a first strike, and the satellite system was new. Ground radar later found no corroboration. The false signal came from sunlight reflected by high clouds in a rare alignment with the satellites.

hist.modern.decolonization.twenty-nine-c.title: Twenty-nine countries, fifty-four per cent of the world
hist.modern.decolonization.twenty-nine-c.hook: Twenty-nine delegations met in a Javanese hill town in 1955 and spoke for more than half of humanity.
hist.modern.decolonization.twenty-nine-c.author: author-humanities-1
hist.modern.decolonization.twenty-nine-c.body: Bandung, West Java, 18 to 24 April 1955. Twenty-nine Asian and African delegations, convened by Indonesia, Burma, India, Ceylon and Pakistan, representing about 1.5 billion people — 54% of the world's population. They agreed ten principles, among them non-intervention, racial equality and the refusal to let collective defence pacts serve great-power interests. Neither bloc had been invited. The Non-Aligned Movement followed at Belgrade in 1961.

recall.question: What made the Bandung Conference of 1955 unusual?
recall.answer: It was a meeting of newly independent Asian and African states with neither Cold War bloc present — 29 delegations speaking for roughly 54% of the world's population — and it produced the ten principles that led to the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.

hist.modern.enlightenment.the-book-that-.title: The Enlightenment was sold on subscription
hist.modern.enlightenment.the-book-that-.hook: Twenty-eight volumes, 71,818 articles, and a business model: you paid before it existed.
hist.modern.enlightenment.the-book-that-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Cut to length and removed unsupported worker-wage comparison.

hist.modern.enlightenment.the-book-that-.body:
The first edition of Diderot and d'Alembert's *Encyclopédie* began appearing in 1751. Its 17 text volumes and 11 volumes of plates cost about 980 livres a set. Buyers subscribed in advance, paying for a work that would take two decades to finish.

That expensive edition sold 4,225 copies and earned its publishers more than two million livres. Cheaper editions followed. By 1789 roughly 25,000 sets in various formats had sold across Europe. Historian Robert Darnton's point is that Enlightenment ideas needed more than brilliant authors: printers, booksellers, subscribers and a business model carried them. The subscription list helped turn a vast manuscript project into something people could actually read.

recall.question: Why does Darnton study the Encyclopédie's accounts rather than only its arguments?
recall.answer: Because the accounts explain the reach. A 4,225-copy first edition at 980 livres was an elite object; the cheaper quarto and octavo reprints put it within the upper middle class, and about 25,000 sets had sold across Europe by 1789.

hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.title: A trucker got bored waiting at the docks
hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.hook: The single object that did most for globalisation is a corrugated steel box with no moving parts.
hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Levinson's figures are $5.83 a ton against 15.8 cents, not $5.86 and 16 cents; corrected in body and recall. McLean's dock epiphany labelled possibly apocryphal, as Levinson does.

hist.modern.globalization.the-metal-box.body:
Malcom McLean ran a trucking company in North Carolina. The story he told was of sitting in a queue at a Hoboken pier in 1937, watching longshoremen move his cargo one sack at a time, and wondering why the whole trailer could not simply be lifted aboard. Marc Levinson, who wrote the book on this, calls that origin story possibly apocryphal.

On 26 April 1956 a converted tanker, the *Ideal-X*, left Newark for Houston carrying 58 metal boxes on its deck. Loading a ship by hand cost about \$5.83 a ton at the time. With containers it cost 15.8 cents. That is not an improvement; it is a different industry.

Everything downstream followed: cranes, standard sizes, ports moving from crowded city waterfronts to open land, dockworker unions gutted, and the cost of distance falling far enough that manufacturing could be split across oceans. Nothing was invented that a nineteenth-century engineer could not have built. The hard part was getting railways, truckers, ports and unions to agree on a box.

recall.question: Why is the container usually credited with more than the ships that carry it?
recall.answer: Because the binding cost was handling, not sailing. Loading by hand ran around \$5.83 a ton; containerised, 15.8 cents. Collapsing that cost is what made splitting production across oceans worth doing.

sources.title: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger
sources.author: Marc Levinson

hist.modern.imperialism.the-conference-t.title: The conference that did not partition Africa
hist.modern.imperialism.the-conference-t.hook: Fourteen delegations, no Africans, and only Congo frontiers addressed. The Berlin Conference did less than its reputation and worse.
hist.modern.imperialism.the-conference-t.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Added 2024 research and narrowed the effective-occupation and border claims.

hist.modern.imperialism.the-conference-t.body:
Bismarck hosted fourteen delegations in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885; no African state was represented. The meeting recognized the Congo Free State's governing association and set Congo basin trade rules. It stated vague rules for new coastal claims.

It did not partition the continent. A 2024 study finds that the conference dealt with Congo frontiers, most revised. The median African colonial border reached its final form in 1908. The classroom map compresses decades of conquest and negotiation into one room, making the violence too easy to miss.

recall.question: What did the Berlin Conference actually decide?
recall.answer: It recognized the Congo governing association, addressed trade in the Congo basin and stated limited rules for new coastal claims. Most African colonial borders were made or revised later, outside the conference.

sources.title: Endogenous Colonial Borders: Precolonial States and Geography in the Partition of Africa
sources.author: Jack Paine, Xiaoyan Qiu and Joan Ricart-Huguet

hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.title: The first thing that ever went viral
hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.hook: Luther was not the first to attack indulgences. He was the first to do it where there was a printing press.
hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Melanchthon's account dated to 1546 and flagged as second-hand (he reached Wittenberg in 1518). Rubin's result quoted as 'at minimum' 29 points, the abstract's wording.

hist.modern.printing-reformation.the-fir.body:
Jan Hus said most of it a century earlier and was burned at Constance in 1415. Martin Luther posted his ninety-five theses on 31 October 1517 — the nailing to the church door is a later embellishment, reported in 1546 by Melanchthon, who did not reach Wittenberg until 1518 — and within weeks the text was in print across the German lands, in Latin and then in German.

The machinery mattered more than the argument. Luther wrote short, cheap, furious pamphlets in the vernacular, and printers, who were businesses, discovered he sold. A trade built on slow Latin bibles became a news industry.

You can test this rather than assert it. Jared Rubin, in 2014, compared German-speaking cities by whether they had a press by 1500, using distance from Mainz — Gutenberg's town — as the instrument. Cities with a press by 1500 were, in Rubin's words, at minimum 29 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600.

The lesson generalises uncomfortably. An idea's spread is not determined only by its truth or its appeal, but by whether the reproduction technology of the moment happens to favour its format.

recall.question: What does Rubin's use of distance from Mainz accomplish in the printing-and-Protestantism study?

options.text: It measures how far Lutheran preachers had to travel
options.why: the instrument is about presses, not preachers.

options.text: It supplies variation in press adoption
options.why: variation plausibly unrelated to a city's religious leanings, so presses can be read as a cause.

options.text: It controls for city size
options.why: size is a covariate in the regression, not what the distance instrument is for.

sources.title: Printing and Protestants: An Empirical Test of the Role of Printing in the Reformation
sources.author: Jared Rubin

hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.title: There was no such thing, and this is a book about it
hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.hook: The best-known book on the Scientific Revolution opens by denying that it happened.
hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Quote confirmed verbatim. The publisher page serves the second edition, so the source now names it; the body keeps 1996 for the first.

hist.modern.scientific-revolution.there-.body:
> "There was no such thing as the Scientific Revolution, and this is a book about it."

Steven Shapin, opening *The Scientific Revolution* (University of Chicago Press, 1996). He is not denying Kepler, Galileo, Boyle or Newton. He is refusing a label that bundles unlike people into one movement with one method — a period name coined long afterwards.

It bites because every field keeps one. The Enlightenment. The Industrial Revolution. The AI revolution. Convenient containers that hide how accidental the contents were.

sources.title: The Scientific Revolution (2nd edition; first published 1996)
sources.author: Steven Shapin

hist.modern.ww1.the-plan-that-may-not-ha.title: The plan that may not have existed
hist.modern.ww1.the-plan-that-may-not-ha.hook: The most famous war plan of the twentieth century may be a thing the losers invented afterwards to explain losing.
hist.modern.ww1.the-plan-that-may-not-ha.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Removed false consensus and an arbitrary event date; recast recall around the real dispute.

hist.modern.ww1.the-plan-that-may-not-ha.body:
The familiar story says Schlieffen left Germany a perfect 1905 blueprint: sweep through Belgium, defeat France, then turn east. His successor Moltke supposedly weakened it and lost the war. After German archives reopened, historian Terence Zuber argued that this tidy plan was largely a postwar construction by officers defending their reputations.

Other historians object. The 1905 memorandum exists, and they disagree about how it related to the multiple deployment plans Germany actually prepared. It even described a war against France alone, unlike the two-front war of 1914. The point is not that no plan existed; it is that the phrase “the Schlieffen Plan” can hide a contested chain of documents, decisions and later excuses.

recall.question: What does the debate over the Schlieffen Plan actually dispute?

options.text: Whether the 1905 memorandum exists
options.why: it does; historians dispute its status and relation to later planning.

options.text: Whether one memorandum was an operational master plan for 1914
options.why: Germany had multiple plans, and historians disagree about how the documents fit together.

options.text: Whether Germany invaded Belgium
options.why: that happened; the dispute concerns planning and later explanations.

hist.science.alchemy-chemistry.a-million.title: A million words on alchemy, sold at auction
hist.science.alchemy-chemistry.a-million.hook: Newton wrote about a million words on alchemy. The papers were auctioned in 1936 and Keynes bought a pile of them.
hist.science.alchemy-chemistry.a-million.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Shortened and added the Newton manuscript collection as a primary source.

hist.science.alchemy-chemistry.a-million.body:
Newton wrote or copied roughly a million words about alchemy. Most of these manuscripts stayed unpublished after his death. In 1936 the Earl of Portsmouth sent 329 lots of Newton's papers to Sotheby's; over a third contained alchemical material.

John Maynard Keynes bought many of them, along with Newton's death mask. Reading the manuscripts led him to call Newton “the last of the magicians.” That line does not erase the *Principia*. It asks us to stop dividing Newton neatly into a modern scientist on one side and a secret hobbyist on the other. Alchemy occupied a serious part of his working life.

recall.question: Why did Keynes call Newton "the last of the magicians"?
recall.answer: Because the manuscripts he bought at the 1936 Sotheby's sale showed Newton spending enormous effort — around a million words — on alchemy and prophecy, pursued with the same seriousness as the *Principia*, not as a hobby separable from it.

hist.science.computing.note-g-and-the-be.title: The footnotes were three times longer than the article
hist.science.computing.note-g-and-the-be.hook: Lovelace was asked to translate someone else's article. Her footnotes came out three times longer than it.
hist.science.computing.note-g-and-the-be.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Shortened, acknowledged the algorithm's error and qualified programming priority.

hist.science.computing.note-g-and-the-be.body:
In 1843 Ada Lovelace translated Luigi Menabrea's account of Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine. Then she added seven notes, together much longer than the article. Note G lays out steps for calculating a Bernoulli number on a machine that had not been built. The published table contains an error; transcribed exactly, it would give the wrong result.

Calling Lovelace the first programmer is contested because Babbage had drafted earlier unpublished programs. Her published Notes still did something striking: they treated the Engine as a machine for manipulating symbols, not merely adding numbers. She also insisted that it could carry out instructions but could not originate ideas on its own.

recall.question: What is the strongest claim to make for Lovelace's Notes?

options.text: That she wrote the first program ever
options.why: Babbage had drafted several dozen unpublished sample programs between 1837 and 1840.

options.text: That she saw the machine as a general symbol processor and published a detailed algorithm
options.why: even though its table contains an error.

options.text: That she designed the Analytical Engine
options.why: the design was Babbage's; her contribution is the Notes.

hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.title: The metre is 0.2 millimetres wrong, and he knew
hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.hook: It was meant to be one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance. It is 0.2 mm off, and the man who knew never said.
hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Arcs corrected: Delambre took Dunkirk-Rodez, Mechain Rodez-Barcelona. Cause of death softened to 'a fever, usually identified as yellow fever'. The 0.197 mm and its cause verified as written.

hist.science.measurement-metric.the-metr.body:
In 1791 revolutionary France decided the new unit of length should belong to nobody: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, along the meridian through Paris. Two astronomers were sent to measure it. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the northern arc, Dunkirk down to Rodez; Pierre Méchain took the southern, Rodez to Barcelona. Both worked through a country at war, arrested repeatedly as suspected spies, carrying instruments that looked exactly like a spy's.

Seven years later Méchain had a problem. His two sets of latitude readings at Barcelona disagreed by more than his instruments should allow. He did not report it. He revised, withheld, agonised, and went back to Spain to fix the arc, where he died in September 1804 of a fever, usually identified as yellow fever.

The metre that came out of the survey is about 0.197 mm shorter than the definition it was chasing, mostly because the survey ignored the deflection of the vertical at its southern end — a gravitational quirk, not Méchain's carelessness. His secret was a real error hiding inside a systematic one.

recall.question: Why is the metre not exactly one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance?
recall.answer: The 1792-99 meridian survey carried a small systematic error, chiefly from ignoring the deflection of the vertical near its southern end, leaving the metre about 0.197 mm short. The unit was kept anyway, and later redefined against a bar, then a wavelength, then the speed of light.

hist.science.medicine.eighteen-point-thr.title: One ward, one rule, a dramatic drop
hist.science.medicine.eighteen-point-thr.hook: April 1847: 18.3% of mothers died in that ward. July, after one new rule: 1.2%. It took the profession decades to accept it.
hist.science.medicine.eighteen-point-thr.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Shortened and removed unsupported claims about universal disbelief and the circumstances of death.

hist.science.medicine.eighteen-point-thr.body:
At Vienna General Hospital, mothers died of puerperal fever far more often in the maternity clinic staffed by doctors and students than in the one staffed by midwives. The doctors also performed autopsies. Ignaz Semmelweis suspected material from cadavers reached patients on their hands.

In mid-May 1847 he ordered washing with chlorinated lime before examinations. Deaths in the First Clinic had reached 18.3% in April; the rate fell to 2.2% in June and 1.2% in July. That dramatic comparison helped him argue for handwashing, but he lacked a germ theory and faced resistance from colleagues. He died in 1865, before his explanation gained broad acceptance.

recall.question: What was Semmelweis's evidence, and why was it resisted?
recall.answer: In the First Clinic, mortality fell from 18.3% in April 1847 to 2.2% in June and 1.2% in July after chlorinated-lime handwashing began. Colleagues resisted a claim for which Semmelweis lacked a germ-based explanation and which implicated their own practice.

hist.science.overview.take-nobodys-word-.title: Take nobody's word for it
hist.science.overview.take-nobodys-word-.hook: The oldest scientific society in continuous existence chose as its motto an instruction not to trust it.
hist.science.overview.take-nobodys-word-.author: author-humanities-1
hist.science.overview.take-nobodys-word-.body: The Royal Society was founded on 28 November 1660 and chartered in 1662. Its motto, taken from Horace, is *Nullius in verba* — take nobody's word for it. The point was not scepticism as a pose but a procedure: settle questions by experiment rather than by citing an authority, including this one. In 1665 it launched *Philosophical Transactions*, the first journal given over entirely to science, and with it the habit of publishing so that strangers can check you.

recall.question: What does *Nullius in verba* commit the Royal Society to?
recall.answer: Deciding questions by experiment instead of by authority — literally "take nobody's word for it", including the Society's own. The founding of *Philosophical Transactions* in 1665 made the checking public.

sources.title: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society

hist.science.statistics.eight-hundred-gu.title: Remember the law of large numbers? Galton took it to a country fair
hist.science.statistics.eight-hundred-gu.hook: Galton's fairground median was startlingly close. Did that prove the law of large numbers?
hist.science.statistics.eight-hundred-gu.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Distinguished published numbers from archival corrections and median from mean; added primary papers.

hist.science.statistics.eight-hundred-gu.body:
Remember the law of large numbers, where averages settle as independent observations accumulate? Francis Galton tried a messier version at a Plymouth livestock show in 1906. He collected 787 valid guesses of an ox's dressed weight. In his 1907 report, the *median* guess was 1,207 pounds; he gave the true weight as 1,198—less than one per cent apart.

Later archival work corrected those figures slightly to 1,208 and 1,197. More crucially, Galton reported a median, while the usual law of large numbers concerns a mean. A crowd is not automatically independent or unbiased. Its answer can be impressively close, but one fairground result does not prove a universal wisdom of crowds.

recall.question: Why does Galton's ox result not directly prove the usual law of large numbers?

options.text: Because the crowd was too small
options.why: 787 entries are ample for an illustration; the mathematical assumptions are the issue.

options.text: Because he highlighted a median from real people, while the usual theorem concerns means under probabilistic assumptions
options.why: a close result alone proves neither independence nor lack of bias.

options.text: Because the ox's weight was unknown
options.why: it was measured after the competition.
